title: Names of the Eucharist (CCC 1328–1332)
hook: Lord's Supper, breaking of bread, holy sacrifice, Holy Communion, Holy Mass

segments.voice: Yesterday, Confirmation's gifts: it deepens, strengthens and sends. Your line was sent.

Evening, on the road to a village called Emmaus. Two disciples are walking out of Jerusalem, heartbroken, and a stranger falls in beside them. He explains the Scriptures to them all the way there. They beg him to stay for supper. At the table he takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them, and in that moment they recognize him, and he vanishes. That same hour they go back to Jerusalem to tell the others. Luke, in the Douay-Rheims, puts it this way: "they knew him in the breaking of bread." That phrase became one of the names for what Catholics celebrate at every Mass. Only one of them.
screen: `TWO DISCIPLES, A STRANGER.` → `BREAD BLESSED AND BROKEN.` → `THEY KNEW HIM.`

segments.voice: This path walked that road on day sixty-nine; today, the names. The Catechism says this sacrament is so rich that no one name can hold it, and each name brings something out. Eucharist means thanksgiving, tied to the Greek words in the Last Supper accounts, where Jesus gives thanks, and to the Jewish blessings that praise God over bread and wine. The Lord's Supper, because of the meal Jesus ate with his disciples the night before he died, and because it looks ahead to the wedding feast of the Lamb. The breaking of bread, the Emmaus name. In Acts it's what the first Christians kept doing; the Douay-Rheims says they persevered "in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers." The memorial of the Lord's Passion and Resurrection. The Holy Sacrifice, because it makes present the one sacrifice of Christ. The Holy and Divine Liturgy, because the Church's whole liturgy finds its center here. The Most Blessed Sacrament, the name for the Eucharist kept in the tabernacle. Holy Communion, because through it people are united to Christ, and to each other in one body. And last, Holy Mass. The name comes from the end of the liturgy, the Catechism says, from the Latin word for sending, missio, because the people are sent out to do God's will in their daily lives. So the familiar name comes from the last line, the dismissal. Each name opens a different window on one thing: thanks, a supper, bread broken, a memorial, a sacrifice, communion, a sending.
screen: `EUCHARIST: THANKSGIVING.` · `THE SUPPER, THE BREAKING OF BREAD.` · `SACRIFICE, LITURGY, COMMUNION.` · `MASS: FROM THE SENDING.`

segments.voice: On each out-breath, say one name, quietly or in your mind: Eucharist, the Lord's Supper, the breaking of bread, the memorial, the Holy Sacrifice, the Divine Liturgy, the Blessed Sacrament, Holy Communion, Holy Mass. Then go back to whichever name caught you and stay with it, asking what it shows that the others don't. If you pray, rest there in thanks.
Names of the Eucharist. Thanksgiving, supper, breaking of bread, memorial, sacrifice, liturgy, sacrament, communion, Mass: many names, each opening a window on one gift. Today's word.
Your line: one gift, many names. Even the everyday name is a sending. That's day one thousand ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics in the Latin rite usually say Mass for the celebration and Holy Communion for receiving; Eastern Catholics speak of the Divine Liturgy, and the reserved Eucharist is called the Blessed Sacrament.

chat.says: Why do Catholics call it Mass? Where does that word even come from?
options: From the Latin for sending: at the end, people are sent out to do God's will in daily life.
It comes from a Latin word for bread, since the Mass is mostly about the meal.
It's from an old word for crowd, because so many people gather on Sundays.
chat.meaning: The Catechism says the name Mass comes from missio, sending, because the liturgy ends by sending people out to do God's will.

notes: Confirm Challoner wording of Luke 24:35 and Acts 2:42.
The meaning of 'Eucharist' (thanksgiving) and the derivation of 'Mass' from missio are both given in CCC 1328 and 1332 themselves, so they stay under the claims rule.
The list of names follows CCC 1328–1332 but is selected (e.g. 'eucharistic assembly' and 'Holy Mysteries' left out for length). Confirm.
Emmaus retold from Luke 24:13–35; 'in the dark' is from 'the day is now far spent' (24:29) plus their same-hour return (24:33); Keeper may soften.
